::: {.callout-important}
## Why this shows up on TMUA

Paper 2 gives you a proof that **looks completely convincing** and asks: *"which line contains the
error?"* (Err1), or it tests whether you recognise a **classic invalid deduction** (Err2). Every line can
be individually true and the argument still be wrong — the flaw is a step that **does not follow**, or one
that is **only valid in a case the proof forgot to rule out**. You are not checking arithmetic; you are
checking *logic*.
:::

<div class="fs-sub">A purported proof is presented; one step is invalid. Read it line by line and ask of each step: "is this true for <em>every</em> case the line above allows?" The error is almost always a hidden division by zero, a lost sign, or an implication used backwards.</div>

## The catalogue — where proofs break

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Dividing by zero

The most common trap. Cancelling a factor $(a-b)$ is only legal when $a-b\neq0$ — but in a "$1=2$" proof,
that factor **is** zero.

$$ab=ac \;\not\Rightarrow\; b=c \quad(\text{false when }a=0)$$

[if a line divides by an expression, check it can't be $0$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Squaring and rooting

Squaring both sides can **add** solutions; taking a square root **loses the $\pm$**.

$$x^2=9\;\Rightarrow\;x=\pm3,\ \text{not just }3$$

[$\sqrt x=x-2$ squared gives $x=1$ or $4$; only $x=4$ works]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Implication used backwards

Assuming $B\Rightarrow A$ because $A\Rightarrow B$ is true. The converse is a **different** statement.

$$A\Rightarrow B \;\text{ does not give }\; B\Rightarrow A$$

[proving "if it rained the ground is wet" then concluding rain from wet ground]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Circular reasoning

A step that **assumes the very thing** being proved. Every line may be true, yet nothing is established.

[a "proof" of $\sqrt2$ irrational that uses "$\sqrt2$ is irrational" partway]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Non-injective functions

*Non-injective* means **not one-to-one**: two different inputs can share one output, so equal outputs need
not mean equal inputs. Spot it with the **horizontal line test** — if any horizontal line meets the graph
more than once, the function is not one-to-one. $\sin$, $\cos$, $x^2$, $|x|$ all fail it.

$$\sin A=\sin B\;\not\Rightarrow\;A=B$$

[$\sin30^\circ=\sin150^\circ$ but $30\neq150$ — the line $y=\tfrac12$ cuts $y=\sin\theta$ twice]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Inequalities and signs

Multiplying an inequality by a quantity of **unknown sign** is invalid — the direction may flip.

$$\tfrac1x<2 \;\not\Rightarrow\; 1<2x \quad(\text{fails when }x<0)$$

[multiply by $x$ only after splitting into $x>0$ and $x<0$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Logs with a base below $1$

$\log_a$ with $0<a<1$ is a **decreasing** function, so taking it of both sides **reverses** the inequality —
and the argument must stay $>0$.

$$\log_a f<\log_a g \iff f>g \quad(0<a<1)$$

[$\log_{1/2}$ of $\left(\tfrac14\right)^n<\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$ — the 2017 P2 Q18 flip (assignment A1)]{.eg}
:::

::::

## How to read a suspect proof

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### The line-by-line test

For each step ask: **"does this follow from the line above, for *every* value that line allows?"** The
first line where the answer is *no* is the error.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The usual suspects, in order

Scan for: **(1)** a division/cancel — is it ever $0$? **(2)** a square root or a squaring — lost sign or
gained root? **(3)** a converse used as if proved. **(4)** the conclusion sneaking into a premise.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Where it shows up (cross-exam)

Err1/Err2 on Paper 2; the same "find the flaw" skill appears in **MAT/STEP** "explain why this argument is
wrong" parts and in the classic fake "$1=2$" proofs.
:::

## The safe move for each trap

Every classic error has a matching **error-free technique**. Spotting the flaw and knowing the right way to
do it are two halves of the same skill — the mark scheme in the class problems gives both.

| The trap | The safe move | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Dividing by a variable (loses a root) | Move everything to one side and **factor** — never divide by something that could be $0$. | $x^2=5x\Rightarrow x(x-5)=0\Rightarrow x=0$ or $5$ |
| Square-rooting (loses the $\pm$) | Write $\sqrt{x^2}=\lvert x\rvert$, so keep **both** signs. | $x^2=9\Rightarrow x=\pm3$ |
| Squaring an equation (adds roots) | Solve, then **substitute every candidate back** into the original and discard the ones that fail. | $\sqrt{2x+3}=x\Rightarrow x=3$ (reject $x=-1$) |
| A trig equation "solved" once | Find the principal value, then **sketch the graph** and read off *all* solutions in the interval. | $\sin\theta=\tfrac12\Rightarrow \theta=30^\circ,\,150^\circ$ |
| Multiplying/dividing an inequality | If the multiplier's sign is unknown, **split into cases** (or multiply by a square, which is $\ge0$); by a negative, **flip** the sign. | $\dfrac1x<2\Rightarrow x<0$ or $x>\tfrac12$ |
| Using the converse | Use an implication **only in its stated direction**; test the actual claim directly. | $x>2\Rightarrow x^2>4$, but **not** the reverse ($x=-3$) |
| Assuming what you're proving | Reach the conclusion from the assumption — **never state it as a reason**. | a "$\sqrt2$ irrational" proof that cites "$\sqrt2$ is irrational" |

## True or false? — test yourself

Each is a claimed deduction. Memorise the verdict; **the *False* ones are exactly the traps Err2 tests.**

| Statement | T / F ? |
|---|:--:|
| If $ab=ac$ then $b=c$. | |
| If $a^2=b^2$ then $a=b$. | |
| If $\sin A=\sin B$ then $A=B$. | |
| If $x^2=9$ then $x=3$. | |
| If $A\Rightarrow B$ is true, then $B\Rightarrow A$ is true. | |
| Dividing both sides of an equation by an expression is always valid. | |
| If every line of an argument is a true statement, the argument must be valid. | |
| Squaring both sides of an equation can introduce solutions the original did not have. | |
| Multiplying both sides of an inequality by a **negative** number reverses the inequality. | |
| An argument that assumes the thing it is trying to prove is invalid (circular). | |

## Proofs of the "true or false?" facts

Decide each verdict above first, then open the key.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answers & proofs
- If $ab=ac$ then $b=c$ — **False**: only **after** $a\neq0$; at $a=0$, $b$ and $c$ can differ.
- If $a^2=b^2$ then $a=b$ — **False**: $a=\pm b$ (e.g. $a=-3,\ b=3$).
- If $\sin A=\sin B$ then $A=B$ — **False**: $\sin$ is not one-to-one ($30^\circ,150^\circ$).
- If $x^2=9$ then $x=3$ — **False**: $x=\pm3$.
- If $A\Rightarrow B$ is true, then $B\Rightarrow A$ is true — **False**: the converse is a separate fact.
- Dividing both sides of an equation by an expression is always valid — **False**: illegal when the divisor could be $0$.
- If every line is a true statement, the argument must be valid — **False**: each line must **follow from** the last; true-but-disconnected or circular is not a proof.
- Squaring both sides can introduce solutions the original did not have — **True**: squaring is one-way, so it can add extraneous roots (check them back).
- Multiplying both sides of an inequality by a **negative** reverses it — **True**: the standard sign rule.
- An argument that assumes the thing it is proving is invalid (circular) — **True**: it establishes nothing.
:::

## Notes

### The horizontal line test — seeing "not one-to-one"

The reason $\sin A=\sin B$ does not force $A=B$ is that $\sin$ is **not one-to-one**. A quick visual check:
draw any **horizontal line** $y=c$; if it meets the graph **more than once**, two different inputs give the
same output, so the function is not one-to-one. Below, one horizontal line meets each graph **twice** —
those two crossings are exactly the two solutions a naive "take the inverse once" would miss.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 6.6))

# sin on [0,360]: y = 1/2 crosses at 30 and 150
t = np.linspace(0, 360, 800)
ax1.plot(t, np.sin(np.radians(t)), lw=2)
ax1.axhline(0.5, color='crimson', lw=1.6, ls='--')
for x in (30, 150):
    ax1.plot(x, 0.5, 'o', color='crimson', ms=7)
    ax1.annotate(f'{x}°', (x, 0.5), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(0, 10),
                 ha='center', color='crimson', fontsize=11)
ax1.set_title(r'$y=\sin\theta$ meets $y=\frac{1}{2}$ twice  →  $\theta=30°$ and $150°$', fontsize=12)
ax1.set_xlim(0, 360); ax1.set_xticks(range(0, 361, 90))
ax1.set_ylim(-1.2, 1.4); ax1.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8); ax1.grid(alpha=0.25)

# x^2: y = 4 crosses at x = -2 and 2
x = np.linspace(-3.2, 3.2, 400)
ax2.plot(x, x**2, lw=2)
ax2.axhline(4, color='crimson', lw=1.6, ls='--')
for xv in (-2, 2):
    ax2.plot(xv, 4, 'o', color='crimson', ms=7)
    ax2.annotate(f'x={xv}', (xv, 4), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(0, 10),
                 ha='center', color='crimson', fontsize=11)
ax2.set_title(r'$y=x^2$ meets $y=4$ twice  →  $x=-2$ and $2$', fontsize=12)
ax2.set_xlim(-3.2, 3.2); ax2.set_ylim(0, 10.5)
ax2.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8); ax2.grid(alpha=0.25)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Whenever a step "cancels" such a function — writing $A=B$ from $\sin A=\sin B$, or $x=3$ from $x^2=9$ — the
horizontal line test is the warning sign that a second solution has been dropped.

### The method: test every step against every case

A suspect proof is designed to look right. Do not read it for *plausibility* — read it for *validity*, one
step at a time.

::: {.keyline}
**1.** Take each line and ask **"does it follow from the line above, for every value allowed so far?"**
&nbsp; **2.** Watch the four hotspots: a **cancel/division** (could it be $0$?), a **square/root** (sign or
extra root?), a **converse** (was it actually proved?), the **conclusion** (did it sneak into a premise?).
&nbsp; **3.** The **first** line that fails is the answer — errors after it don't matter.
:::

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Find the first error in this "proof" that $2=1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** Let $a=b$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Then $a^2=ab$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** So $a^2-b^2=ab-b^2$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** Factor: $(a-b)(a+b)=b(a-b)$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(5)** Divide by $(a-b)$: $\;a+b=b$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(6)** Since $a=b$: $\;2b=b$, so $2=1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Line (5).** Since $a=b$, the factor $a-b=0$, so dividing by $(a-b)$ is dividing by zero. Lines (1)–(4)
are all valid; the argument collapses precisely at the cancel. $\;\blacksquare$

*The tell: a cancel of a factor that an earlier line has forced to be $0$.*
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### Extraneous solutions — the squaring trap

The key is to read each step as one of two kinds of arrow:

- $\Rightarrow$ (**one-way** — "this follows"): the next line is true whenever this one is, but *not*
  necessarily the reverse. Squaring is one-way: $x=y\Rightarrow x^2=y^2$, but $x^2=y^2$ does **not** give
  $x=y$ (take $x=-3,\,y=3$).
- $\Leftrightarrow$ (**two-way** — "same solutions"): each line has exactly the same solution set as the
  last. Rearranging and factoring are two-way.

A one-way step can *enlarge* the solution set — it may drag in values that never solved the original. That
is why, after any squaring, you must **substitute back** and discard whatever fails.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} A student solves $\sqrt{x}=x-2$ and concludes $x=1$ or $x=4$. What is the error?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** $\sqrt x=x-2$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Square: $x=(x-2)^2=x^2-4x+4$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** So $x^2-5x+4=0$, i.e. $(x-1)(x-4)=0$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** Therefore $x=1$ or $x=4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Label each step $\Rightarrow$ (one-way) or $\Leftrightarrow$ (two-way):

- **(1) $\Rightarrow$ (2)** &nbsp; *one-way (squaring).* If $\sqrt x=x-2$ then $x=(x-2)^2$ — a **true**
  implication. So **line (2) contains no error**; transforming the equation this way is a normal, legal
  move.
- **(2) $\Leftrightarrow$ (3)** &nbsp; *two-way.* Rearranging to $x^2-5x+4=0$ and factoring keeps exactly
  the same solutions — both lines true.
- **(3) $\Rightarrow$ (4)** &nbsp; The quadratic's roots really are $x=1$ or $4$ — correct **for the
  quadratic**. But because step (1)$\Rightarrow$(2) was only one-way, these are just **candidates** for the
  original equation, not guaranteed solutions. **Line (4)** declares them solutions of (1) *without
  checking* — that unjustified leap is the error.

Substitute back into (1): $x=4$ gives $\sqrt4=2=4-2$ ✓; $x=1$ gives $\sqrt1=1$ but $1-2=-1$ ✗. So $x=1$ is
extraneous and only $x=4$ solves the original. $\;\blacksquare$

**Why not line (2)?** Squaring never states anything false — it only widens the net from $\Leftrightarrow$
to $\Rightarrow$. The mistake is keeping the *whole* catch as the answer at (4) without the back-check.

*Whenever a proof squares both sides, the missing step is "check each solution in the original".*
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### Log inequalities when the base is a fraction

Assignment A1 (2017 P2 Q18) hides a sign flip inside a logarithm: the student takes $\log_{1/2}$ of both
sides of $\left(\tfrac14\right)^n<\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$ and *keeps* the "$<$". The reason it breaks
is the **base**. A logarithm $\log_a x$ is **increasing** when $a>1$ but **decreasing** when $0<a<1$: with a
fractional base, as $x$ grows the output *falls*. The picture below is the whole idea — $\log_{1/2}$ is just
$\log_2$ reflected in the $x$-axis.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "y=log₂x (base>1) rises; y=log_{1/2}x (base<1) falls — it is the reflection in the x-axis. For log_{0.5}x>2, the decreasing curve is above y=2 only on 0<x<0.25 (shaded); the argument must also stay >0."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
INC='#bdbdbd'; DEC='#1f77b4'; L='#d62728'; SH='#2ca02c'
x=np.linspace(0.02,4,600)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0,3.8))
ax.plot(x,np.log2(x),color=INC,lw=1.8,ls='--',label='base 2 (>1): increasing')
ax.plot(x,-np.log2(x),color=DEC,lw=2.2,label='base ½ (<1): decreasing')
ax.axhline(2,color=L,ls=':',lw=1.4)
ax.text(3.1,2.15,'y = 2',color=L,fontsize=10)
# log_{1/2}x = 2  <=>  x = 0.25
ax.plot(0.25,2,'o',color=SH,ms=7); ax.annotate('(0.25, 2)',(0.25,2),(0.4,2.6),color=SH,fontsize=10)
ax.axvspan(0.001,0.25,ymin=0.0,ymax=1.0,color=SH,alpha=0.12)
ax.text(0.02,-2.6,'0 < x < 0.25\n(log$_{1/2}$x > 2)',color=SH,fontsize=9)
ax.axvline(0,color='0.55',lw=1.0)  # x=0 asymptote
ax.axhline(0,color='0.7',lw=0.7)
ax.set_xlim(-0.15,4); ax.set_ylim(-3.4,3.6)
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y'); ax.legend(fontsize=8,loc='upper right')
ax.set_title(r'$y=\log_{1/2}x$ is decreasing — so removing it flips the inequality',fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Two things must happen every time, and Err2 is built on forgetting either one.

::: {.keyline}
**1. Flip the sign.** For $0<a<1$, dropping the log **reverses** the inequality:
$$\log_a f(x)<\log_a g(x)\iff f(x)>g(x),\qquad \log_a f(x)<b\iff f(x)>a^{b}.$$
&nbsp; **2. Keep the argument positive.** A logarithm only exists for a positive argument, so **intersect**
with $f(x)>0$. When the flip produces an *upper* bound, the "$>0$" **lower** bound is the easy thing to lose.
:::

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Solve $\log_{0.5}x>2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Base $0.5<1$, so $\log_{0.5}$ is **decreasing** — removing it **reverses** the "$>$":
$$\log_{0.5}x>2\iff x<0.5^{2}=0.25.$$
Now bring in the domain: the argument must satisfy $x>0$. Intersecting the two,
$$\boxed{\,0<x<0.25\,}.$$

*Writing only "$x<0.25$" is the trap — it wrongly admits $x=-1$, where $\log_{0.5}x$ is not even defined. The
flip **and** the domain are both needed.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Core checklist — a log inequality with base $<1$**

- Did you **reverse** the inequality direction when you removed the log?
- Did you **intersect** with the condition that **every argument is $>0$**?
:::

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Solve $\log_{1/3}(x-1)>1$. *(Answer form: an inequality / interval.)*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Base $\tfrac13<1$: decreasing, so flip the "$>$" on removing the log:
$$\log_{1/3}(x-1)>1\iff x-1<\left(\tfrac13\right)^{1}=\tfrac13\iff x<\tfrac43.$$
Domain: the argument $x-1>0$, i.e. $x>1$. Intersecting,
$$\boxed{\,1<x<\tfrac43\,}.$$

*Same two moves: flip because the base is below $1$, then cut down to where $x-1>0$. Drop the domain and you
would include values like $x=0$, where $x-1=-1<0$ and the log does not exist.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::
